In every society there is a class whose members are exempt from useful work and whose standing depends on displaying that exemption. Its members spend lavishly, not primarily because the goods give them pleasure, but because the expenditure itself signals wealth; and the signal works only if the spending is visibly wasteful. Fashions change quickly for this reason: an article that becomes cheap or common ceases to serve as a mark of distinction. The habit spreads downward, since each class takes its standard from the one above it, and a household of modest means may deny itself necessities in order to keep up appearances. The result is an economy that mistakes display for welfare and spends its energy on the production of things that few people genuinely need.
